Rover: slope and roughness differences within the measurement error of the elevation models score as equal, so 254 sites tie at the top; the five are a geographic spread of the 241 tied sites that are not mostly ice or water.
Solar panels: the likeness is of sunlight above the atmosphere; on Earth a large share is lost in the atmosphere, so this is not a likeness of what panels would collect.
Lunar base: a likeness of thermal position within each world's population, not of temperature: the coldest temperatures of the five pairs are 202.9 to 208.6 K apart.

suitability_criterion_clear_sky.product: ISCCP H-series Basic HGM (Gridded Monthly Mean) - cldamt 'Mean cloud amount' (NOAA NCEI Climate Data Record)
suitability_criterion_clear_sky.caveat: ISCCP-H HGM v01r00 (NOAA NCEI) mean clear-sky fraction 2012-2016, 1 - cloud amount; DERIVED; least reliable over snow, ice and polar night; cloud amount is not irradiance
suitability_criterion_clear_sky.text_on_screen: The Solar panels suitability no longer uses criteria driven by latitude. The maximum sun elevation and the share of time with a low sun (pure geometry of latitude) and the modelled ground irradiance (WorldClim, which repeats what the similarity already compares) carry no weight now; their gates still apply, and the ground irradiance, the sunlight above the atmosphere and the share lost stay in every pair's sentence. In their place, the clear-sky fraction measured by satellite makes up half of the suitability (50 %: its weight 0.35 out of the 0.70 that the four weights add up to; the suitability is divided by that sum): 1 minus the mean ISCCP-H cloud amount (NOAA NCEI, monthly means 2012 to 2016), scored from 0 at 0.308 to 1 at 0.671, the 10th and 90th percentiles over the 18,777 points that pass the funnel. 3 of those points have no cloud value and that weight is shared among the other criteria. One of them, the cell at 4.5 S 122.5 E (in Sulawesi, Indonesia, number 16 in the full ranking, suitability 96.23), ranks that high only because its clear-sky weight is shared among the other criteria; it is not among the five shown.

solar.saturation_text_on_screen: The Solar panels similarity is saturated. Sunlight above the atmosphere depends on latitude only, so almost every Earth point finds many cells of the equatorial maria that match it almost exactly: its twin is the best of a median of about 1,840 candidate cells that pass the tolerances, 78 % of the 6,360 pairs score 99 or more and 514 show 100.00. Here a high similarity says that the pair is within the tolerances, not that it is closer than another pair: read the real differences shown beside it (sunlight above the atmosphere, slope and roughness). Among the 100 best-ranked points the similarity only goes from 99.00 to 100.00, so their order follows suitability.

00_welcome.text: Welcome to Stars Beside You, a planetary twin finder. Before a rover, a solar panel or a lunar base ever reaches the Moon, it can be tested here on Earth, if we find the right place. We compare lunar data from NASA missions with data from all over the Earth, and look for a lunar twin for each Earth site. There are three missions. Press one for the Rover, matched on slope and roughness. Press two for Solar panels, matched mainly on sunlight. Press three for the Lunar base, matched mainly on the coldest temperature and the daily swing.

m1_rover.text: Rover. We match places on slope and roughness only. On the Moon we search the south polar region, from 75 degrees south to the pole, where NASA plans to look for water ice. Almost every site differs from its lunar twin by less than the elevation data can measure, so the likeness cannot tell them apart; 254 of them also get full marks, or nearly, on our Rover criteria. Here are five of the 254 sites tied at the top of our model, chosen to be spread across the world. Press one to five to hear each one, or Escape to go back.

numbers.source: rover zone lat_max (zone name on screen: 75°S–90°S)

m2_solar.text: Solar panels. A solar panel lives on sunlight, so we match mainly on the sunlight that arrives each day above the atmosphere. On the Moon we search the low, flat maria within 30 degrees of the equator, where the Sun stands high. Here are five of the highest-scoring analogs in our model, ordered by the final score: half likeness and half suitability. Almost every top site matches its twin's sunlight almost exactly, so the likeness is nearly the same for all of them, and suitability, led by clear skies, decides the order. Press one to five to hear each one, or Escape to go back.

m3_base.text: Lunar base. A base must endure the cold, so we match mainly on the coldest temperature and the daily swing. On the Moon we search NASA's nine candidate landing regions in the south polar region, where NASA plans crewed landings. The Moon is far colder than Earth, so we compare position, not temperature: how each site ranks among Earth's 2,419 candidates, and its twin among the 280 lunar cells of those regions. Here are five of the highest-scoring analogs in our model, ordered by the final score: half likeness and half suitability. Press one to five to hear each one, or Escape to go back.
